title: The Precariat
abstract: Neo-liberal policies and institutional changes have produced a huge and growing number of people with sufficiently common experiences to be called an emerging class. In this book Guy Standing introduces what he calls the Precariat - a growing number of people across the world living and working precariously, usually in a series of short-term jobs, without recourse to stable occupational identities or careers, stable social protection or protective regulations relevant to them. They include migrants, but also locals. Standing argues that this class of people could produce new instabilities in society. They are increasingly frustrated and dangerous because they have no voice, and hence they are vulnerable to the siren calls of extreme political parties. He outlines a new kind of good society, with more people actively involved in civil society and the precariat re-engaged. He goes on to consider one way to a new better society -- an unconditional basic income for everyone, contributed by the state, which could be topped up through earned incomes. This is a topical, and a radical book, which will appeal to a broad market concerned by the increasing problems of labour insecurity and civic disengagement.

narrative:
Short impact summary

The Precariat (2011), published by Bloomsbury Publishing Plc., has been cited 1,939 times — enough that OpenAlex puts it in the top 1% of works in its field and year. Beyond that, it has been downloaded 14,231 times.

Full narrative

The Precariat by Guy Standing was published by Bloomsbury Publishing Plc. in 2011. Conceptually, the work connects to Sociology, Political science, Economic growth and Economics.

OpenAlex records 1,939 citations. That places it in the top 1% of works in its field and year of publication. Citations peaked in 2025 with 179 citing works. Notable citing venues include Open Book Publishers, Journal of Youth Studies and Development and Change. The citing works include 1,407 journal articles, 408 book chapters and 19 books. They come from 40 countries, led by the United Kingdom, the United States and Australia.

It has been downloaded 14,231 times via OAPEN. Open Library reports a combined count of 6 reading logs and catalog editions. Its subject matter aligns with Reduced inequalities among the Sustainable Development Goals.
